findings.explanation: google_kms_crypto_key.cluster is the key used for database_encryption on google_container_cluster.cluster (wired via module.cluster.tf:17 key_name = google_kms_crypto_key.cluster.id -> cluster.tf database_encryption.key_name), i.e. the key that encrypts Kubernetes Secrets at the etcd layer. Its IAM binding (kms.tf:28-35) correctly grants roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter to the GKE control-plane service agent (service-PROJECT_NUMBER@container-engine-robot.iam.gserviceaccount.com, the only identity GCP requires for this), but ALSO grants it to module.cluster.service_account.email — the node pool's own custom service account (google_service_account.default), the identity every node's kubelet runs as. Nodes/kubelet have no legitimate need to decrypt the etcd secrets-encryption key; the analogous binding for the node-pool boot-disk key (kms.tf:37-43) correctly grants only the Compute Engine service agent, not this SA, confirming the .cluster binding is the outlier. If a node or a workload capable of exfiltrating the node's credentials (e.g. via a container escape, since workload_metadata_config already restricts direct pod access to GKE_METADATA-brokered identities) is compromised, it gains a documented path to decrypt the key protecting every Secret in the cluster — a direct escalation past the database_encryption control that's otherwise correctly configured.
findings.remediation: Remove "serviceAccount:${module.cluster.service_account.email}" from google_kms_crypto_key_iam_binding.cluster's members list (kms.tf:33) unless there is a documented reason the node pool SA needs to decrypt the etcd encryption key directly — none is evident from this configuration.
findings.title: Node pool's own service account is granted decrypt access to the cluster's etcd/secrets encryption key
